_comment: Curated prompts for assets that have already been generated and visually approved. build-manifest.mjs uses these verbatim in place of anything it would derive from the design docs, so rebuilding the manifest can never silently replace known-good artwork with a reworded prompt.

Cinematic key art for a AAA mystery adventure game. A lone granite lighthouse tower, one hundred and twelve feet, standing on a wave-broken reef nine miles offshore under a bruised late-October dusk. Its lantern is DARK — no beam. In the near foreground, out of focus, the slate roofline and chimney stacks of a Victorian records fortress on a headland, one small window lit warm amber. Cold Atlantic swell, spindrift, low ragged cloud, a last cold band of dying light on the horizon. Deep teal and slate blues against a single warm amber accent. Painterly digital oil painting, visible confident brushwork, dramatic chiaroscuro, atmospheric depth haze, cinematic wide composition with generous empty sky in the upper third for a title to sit. Moody, lonely, forensic. Absolutely no text, no lettering, no words, no numbers, no signatures, no watermarks, no logos, no UI elements, no borders or frames, no people, no boats.

A soft black radial vignette on a pure white background, heavy darkening at the four corners fading smoothly to clear white at the centre, very gradual falloff, no hard edge, no banding. Pure greyscale gradient only. Absolutely no text, no lettering, no objects, no watermarks, no borders.

Character portrait for a mystery adventure game. Sabine Ferrier-Kyne, Warden of the Brannock Pilotage Authority (appointed 1991), presiding over its dissolution, 58 (b. 12 January 1940). Tall and narrow and upright as a plumb line, five foot ten, no stoop at all at fifty-eight. Iron-grey hair cut short and set once a fortnight, combed straight back off a high bony forehead. A long face; deep vertical folds from nose to mouth; pale grey eyes with slightly slack lower lids; a wide thin mouth. Big-knuckled hands, nails cut square and short, no varnish, a thin gold wedding band worn on the right hand since she was widowed in 1991. Wears three things in rotation: a charcoal wool skirt suit with a faintly military shoulder, a cream blouse with a small round collar, and a cardigan the colour of wet slate kept over the shoulders indoors like a stole. A 2H pencil behind the right ear at all times, sharpened with a blade, never a sharpener. Reading glasses on a black cord. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: a small, entirely genuine, entirely attentive smile that arrives about half a second late, as though she had to finish a sentence in her head first. Bearing and expression: The most competent person in any room she has ever been in, and the only one who has never once said so. Courteous to the point of being unanswerable. Character portrait for a mystery adventure game. Halvard Pike, Chief Clerk, 66 (b. 1932). Short and heavy through the chest, five foot six, stooped from forty years of hauling boxes off high shelves. Bald across the crown with grey hair combed flat across it and grey hair in the ears. A bulbous, broken-veined nose; small wet blue eyes; a permanent shaving cut on the left jaw. Brown cotton warehouse coat over a shirt and a knitted maroon tie, sleeve garters above the elbow, cuffs gone shiny. Thick-lensed National Health spectacles mended at the left hinge with copper wire. Ineradicable purple ink on the first two fingers of the right hand and a nail on the right thumb split by a box lid in 1979. Bearing and expression: Rude on principle and correct on detail. Wiry and weathered, five foot four, forearms and hands like a boatwoman's, knuckles thickened. Dark hair going iron at the temples, cut short by herself with kitchen scissors and never quite level. Broad flat face, high colour across the cheekbones, a white scar through the left eyebrow from a davit in 1988. Navy fisherman's smock over a fleece, black oilskin trousers, sea boots turned down at the top, a brass whistle on a green lanyard. Nicotine on the first two fingers, a roll-up behind the ear in the dry. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: jaw set, chin slightly up, eyes going past your shoulder to look at the weather. Soft white hair in a low bun held with a tortoiseshell comb, wisps escaping at the nape. A face made almost entirely of kind creases; pale blue eyes behind gold half-moon spectacles on a beaded chain; a slight tremor in the left hand she has had since 1989. Lilac twinset, pleated tweed skirt, thick brown tights, a wedding ring worn to a wire. Character portrait for a mystery adventure game. Dr Ivo Sandbach, Conservation architect and project manager, Sandbach & Roule, for the conversion of Pilotage House into a heritage hotel, 44 (b. 1954). Big and soft-handed, six foot two, going heavy round the middle. Sandy hair receding, cut expensively in a town nobody here has been to. Ruddy and handsome in a bruised way; blue eyes; three days of stubble by Act III. Quilted olive gilet over a checked shirt, cord trousers, brand-new steel-toed boots that are not dirty until the night of the crowbar. Carries a hard hat and never wears it, a Nokia the size of a brick, and an A3 drawings tube with a photograph of two girls aged nine and twelve rolled inside it. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: cheerful, and about fifteen per cent too fast. Bearing and expression: A man doing sums in his head while he talks to you. Genuinely knowledgeable about lime mortar and genuinely uninterested in anything that is not on the programme. Bullies with jokes. For four acts, a voice on a bakelite handset and a passport photograph clipped inside the cover of Wren's casebook: silver hair in a severe bob, reading glasses pushed up into it, a hawk's face, a mustard scarf. At the Board on 3 November she is present in person: tweed, a plaster cast to the hip, a stick in each hand, and a walking frame parked six feet away which she has refused to touch since Tuesday. Character portrait for a mystery adventure game. Cormac Sallow, Lamp Superintendent of the Brannock Pilotage Authority 1958–1984, 79 at death (b. 1919, d. 14 September 1998). Present only as a three-quarter oil in the Lamp Superintendents' frame in the Lamp Room, painted 1979 against a dark ground exactly like the Wardens on the Great Stair, and as one police photograph in the coroner's file that the game lets you look at once. Big-boned and heavy-shouldered, six foot one and stooped by the end; white hair in a brush cut; a face like a weathered cliff, deep-set brown eyes, a jaw that has been broken; enormous scarred hands with two fingers missing the top joints from a lantern gear in 1962. A knitted waistcoat over a collarless shirt, a hearing aid in the right ear with the cord tucked into the waistcoat. Painted expression: patient, faintly amused, waiting for you to catch up. Bearing and expression: Reconstructed entirely from paper and from other people's grief: methodical, literal, kind in an undemonstrative way, incapable of exaggeration, and — the fatal quality — trusting of documents.
